title: I'm Surprised
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short piece dissects a single linguistic tool leaders can use to deliver critical feedback without triggering the alarm that direct criticism causes: the phrase 'I'm surprised.' The author works through several example sentences to show how the phrase signals a violated expectation while leaving space for the recipient to ask why, which typically prompts the offender to generate their own accountability conversation. A useful caveat closes the piece: the same phrase used after a strong outcome reads as a backhanded insult rather than praise, so context is essential to using it well.
points: The phrase 'I'm surprised' delivers critical feedback indirectly, softening disappointment while still making the disapproval unmistakable.
Because it's hard for the recipient not to ask why the leader was surprised, the phrase often prompts the offender to generate their own direct feedback discussion.
Used after a strong outcome, the same phrase reads as a backhanded insult rather than a compliment, so context and timing matter enormously.
The technique works because expressing surprise signals a violated expectation without requiring the leader to state the criticism outright.
quotes: Leaders who express disappointment in people can unintentionally create a tsunami of doubt and insecurity.
When used to convey feedback, the expression “I’m surprised” carries a payload of disappointment powerfully but indirectly.

In each case, the expression of surprise indirectly conveys disagreement or distaste. But the power of the expression lies in the fact that it is exceedingly difficult for those on the receiving end not to inquire about why the leader was surprised.
But be careful not to use the expression after a good outcome or competent performance. In that context, “I’m surprised” is a back-handed compliment at best and an insult at worst.
Frankly, we’re surprised you haven’t considered the full power of this phrase before.
